the spectral change between the XMM-2004 and XMM-2008 observations is not associated with an increase in the X-ray flux, and that the X-ray flux during the 2008-2009 outburst is not consistent with the X-ray emission from an intermediate-mass accreting black hole.
the X-ray properties of HLX1 are consistent with both scenarios, and that the X-ray luminosities and distances of the two sources are not well constrained.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HLX1 system remains an enigmatic object, and that the evidence for an intermediate-mass (or even supermassive) black hole is not conclusive.

the X-ray data are consistent with either an intermediate-mass BH or with a neutron star, but the neutron star scenario is more likely, and that there is no clear evidence for an intermediate-mass or super-massive black hole in HLX1.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the XMM-2008 and Swift-2009 observations of HLX-1 are equally consistent with a foreground neutron-star scenario as they are with an intermediate-mission black hole in a low/hard state, and that the X-ray luminosities of the 2008 and 2009 outbursts were not significantly different.
the HLX1 source is not unique, as the X-ray spectral properties of HLX1 are similar to those of a few neutron stars in the Milky Way and the LMC.
the X-ray properties of HLX1 do not provide any strong evidence for an intermediate-mass (or supermassive) black hole.
